items.title: Composite midpoint rule on a uniform grid
items.statement:
Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and a function $f$. If $a\ge b$
or $n<1$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the remaining inputs,
require a real-valued function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ evaluable at every point
of $[a,b]$. Put $h=(b-a)/n$ and $m_j=a+(j+\tfrac12)h$ for $0\le j<n$. The
composite midpoint rule returns

$$Q_M(f;a,b,n):=h\sum_{j<n} f(m_j).$$

The sum is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. The admissibility conditions
$a<b$ and $n\ge1$ ensure $h>0$ and all $m_j\in(a+jh,a+(j+1)h)$. The rule is an
exact-real formula; floating-point evaluation and summation error are separate
from its quadrature error.
items.strategy: A finite exact-real weighted sum; invalid intervals or panel counts return an explicit status.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.1
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Composite Simpson rule on an even uniform grid
items.statement:
Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and an evaluation function $f$.
If $a\ge b$ or $n<2$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the
remaining inputs require $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ to be evaluable at every
point of $[a,b]$. If $n$ is odd, the procedure returns
invalid-Simpson-panel-count. If $n$ is even, put
$h=(b-a)/n$ and $x_j=a+jh$ for $0\le j\le n$; return

$$Q_S(f;a,b,n):=\frac h3\sum_{j<n/2}\bigl(f(x_{2j})+4f(x_{2j+1})+f(x_{2j+2})\bigr).$$

The sum is a finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. Each two-panel block
$[x_{2j},x_{2j+2}]$ uses its endpoints and midpoint. Expanding the block sum
gives weights $1,4,2,\ldots,4,1$. The even condition
$n\ge2$ makes the number of blocks a positive integer. The formula is an exact-real
procedure; floating point evaluation and summation error are separate from
its quadrature error.
items.strategy: A finite exact-real weighted sum over n/2 two-panel blocks.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.2
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Midpoint panel error kernel and second-derivative bound
items.statement:
Let $a<b$, $m=(a+b)/2$, and $f\in C^2([a,b])$ in the sense of
[[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Define

$$K(t)=\begin{cases}\frac12(t-a)^2,&a\le t\le m,\\\frac12(b-t)^2,&m\le t\le b.\end{cases}$$

Then $K$ is nonnegative and continuous,

$$\int_a^b f(t)\,dt-(b-a)f(m)=\int_a^b K(t)f''(t)\,dt,$$

and, with $M_2:=\max_{t\in[a,b]}|f''(t)|$,

$$\left|\int_a^b f(t)\,dt-(b-a)f(m)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)^3}{24}M_2.$$

In particular, if $f''\ge0$ on $[a,b]$, the panel midpoint value does not
exceed the integral.
items.strategy: Apply integration by parts twice on the two half-panels, then use kernel positivity and its exact integral.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.1
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Composite midpoint error bound for a twice continuously differentiable function
items.statement:
Let $a<b$, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^2([a,b])$, define $M_2=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f''(x)|$. The composite
midpoint value $Q_M(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-midpoint-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_M(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^2}{24}M_2.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.
items.strategy: Apply the local midpoint kernel estimate to every panel, use additivity, and sum the panel bounds.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, Theorem 7.1
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Peano kernel identity for one Simpson panel
items.statement:
Let $a<b$, put $L=b-a$ and $m=(a+b)/2$, and let $f\in C^4([a,b])$. Define
the one-block Simpson value and its kernel by

$$S(f;a,b):=\frac{L}{6}\bigl(f(a)+4f(m)+f(b)\bigr),\qquad K_{a,b}(x):=\begin{cases}\frac{(x-a)^3(3(x-a)-2L)}{72},&a\le x\le m,\\\frac{(b-x)^3(3(b-x)-2L)}{72},&m\le x\le b.\end{cases}$$

Then

$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-S(f;a,b)=\int_a^bK_{a,b}(x)f^{(4)}(x)\,dx,$$

and $K_{a,b}\le0$ with
$\int_a^b|K_{a,b}(x)|\,dx=L^5/2880$. The value $S(f;a,b)$ is the one-block
specialization of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]].
items.strategy: Integrate by parts four times on each half, compute the jump contribution at the midpoint, and integrate the kernel.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.2
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Composite Simpson rule is exact through cubic degree
items.statement:
Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and let
$p(x)=c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2+c_3x^3$ with real coefficients. Then

$$\int_a^b p(x)\,dx=Q_S(p;a,b,n),$$

where $Q_S$ is the composite Simpson value of
[[alg-composite-simpson-rule]].
items.strategy: The Peano kernel identity has zero remainder when the fourth derivative vanishes; sum over the two-panel blocks.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.2
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Composite Simpson error bound for a four-times continuously differentiable function
items.statement:
Let $a<b$, let $n\ge2$ be an even integer, and put $h=(b-a)/n$. If
$f\in C^4([a,b])$, set $M_4=\max_{x\in[a,b]}|f^{(4)}(x)|$. Then the value
$Q_S(f;a,b,n)$ of [[alg-composite-simpson-rule]] satisfies

$$\left|\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-Q_S(f;a,b,n)\right|\le\frac{(b-a)h^4}{180}M_4.$$

The integral is the Riemann integral. This is an exact-arithmetic quadrature
bound; evaluation and summation roundoff are not included.
items.strategy: Scale the one-panel Peano kernel to every two-panel block, add the block errors, and use the triangle inequality.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.2
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Convex data bracket the integral between composite midpoint and trapezoid values
items.statement:
Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be convex and Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$, with
$a<b$, and let $n\ge1$ be an integer. Then

$$Q_M(f;a,b,n)\le\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\le T_n(f),$$

where $Q_M$ is the composite midpoint value and $T_n(f)$ is the published
composite trapezoidal value of [[def-composite-trapezoidal-rule]] on the same
interval and uniform grid. Darboux integrability is the explicit premise that
makes the displayed Riemann integral defined. The proof uses convexity directly
for both inequalities and assumes no differentiability.
items.strategy: Reflect each panel to prove its midpoint lower bound from convexity, and integrate its endpoint chord for the upper bound.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.1
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Simpson rule integrates a quadratic exactly on one two-panel block
items.statement:
On $[0,2]$, the function $f(x)=x^2$ has exact integral $8/3$. With $n=2$,
$h=1$, and the composite Simpson rule,

$$Q_S(f;0,2,2)=\frac13\bigl(f(0)+4f(1)+f(2)\bigr)=\frac83.$$

This is the quadratic case of exactness through degree three.
items.strategy: Evaluate the antiderivative and the three Simpson node values.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.2
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6

items.title: Simpson rule integrates a cubic exactly on one two-panel block
items.statement:
On $[0,2]$, let $f(x)=x^3$. With $n=2$ and $h=1$, the Simpson value is

$$Q_S(f;0,2,2)=\frac13\bigl(f(0)+4f(1)+f(2)\bigr)=4,$$

which equals the exact integral $\int_0^2x^3\,dx=4$. The full two-panel block
is exact because the rule annihilates the Peano remainder of every cubic.
items.strategy: Evaluate the antiderivative and the three Simpson node values.

references.title: Art B. Owen, Monte Carlo Theory, Methods and Examples, Chapter 7, §7.2
Tobin A. Driscoll and Richard J. Braun, Fundamentals of Numerical Computation, §5.6
